catalog_quote: Like English, Yugambeh is 'stress-timed', as are the other dialects of this language. The prominent syllables and words take more time, and the unstressed words and syllables are often slurred over. ... You should note that the first syllable of a word is usually stressed and clear, except when there is a long vowel elsewhere in the word, which then gets the primary stress, and the first syllable is less clear. ... You will note that there are long and short vowels. Short e is rather rare, although it sometimes alternates with i or a word finally. Unstressed vowels in the language lose their 'colour', as they do in English. Long vowels (all the ones with h written after them) are stressed; otherwise the first syllable of a word is stressed. There are never (or almost never) two long vowels in a row. [Sharpe 1998:14-15, 17] ... An acute accent indicates stress usually when it falls on ot…

new_statements.rule_in_words: Holmer states only that syllabic (word) stress is non-phonemic, i.e. not contrastive, in the Coraki/Bungawalbin Bandjalang dialect, while vowel length is phonemic; he gives no rule for where stress falls. (Sharpe 1997:372, for the whole Yugambeh-Bundjalung chain including Lower Richmond, implies default first-syllable stress with a long vowel elsewhere attracting the perceived stress; Holmer 1983 §2.9, for his Queensland survey languages only, notes a tendency to stress the second syllable of long words.)
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in Holmer 1971. Holmer 1983 (Queensland languages, not this one) mentions secondary stress on alternate syllables after the second.
new_statements.exceptions: None in Holmer 1971. Sharpe 1997:372 (pan-dialect): stress falls on other than the first syllable when that syllable has a long vowel.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('Syllabic stress'); the only other use of 'stressed' in the book is a sentence-level remark that clitic particles follow 'a stressed word toward the beginning of the sentence'. Data = 1964 field notes from two speakers (EF: Coraki/Bungawalbin; BT), i.e. citation and text forms.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog lowe1444 'Lower Richmond' = Sharpe's Lower Richmond group (Nyangbal, Wiyabal, Coraki Bandjalang, Galibal); dialects in Glottolog: Bandjalang [band1358] (Coraki/Bungawalbin, Sharpe's 'Wuyebal'/BJ), Wiyabal [wiya1239] (Lismore), Njangbal [njan1241] (Ballina/Cabbage Tree Island). Holmer 1971 describes the Coraki/Bungawalbin speech of Mrs Evelyn Ferguson (EF) plus a second speaker (BT); Holmer 1983 calls it 'the Lismore and Bungawalbin Bandjalang', so the statement covers band1358 (and possibly wiya1239). The Sharpe 1997 stress remark is for the whole Yugambeh-Bundjalung chain, and Crowley 1978 / StressTyp2 / WALS 'Bandjalang' statements are for Waalubal [waal1238] of Middle Clarence [midd1357], not this language.

sources.note: p.372 (the text layer), said of Watson's diacritics but stated for the whole dialect chain: 'An acute accent indicates stress usually when it falls on other than the first syllable. By Crowley's, the Geytenbeeks' and my analysis, this indicates a long vowel in the syllable perceived as stressed.' p.373: 'where the stress patterns of the language force a vowel shortening'. Defines Lower Richmond = Nyangbal, Wiyabal, Coraki Bandjalang, Galibal (p.~370, line 362) and uses Holmer 1971 as the Wiyabal/Wuyebal (Lismore/Coraki) source (WI/BJ).
